strokes.label: Stroke code
strokes.keys: Type strokes. <kbd>Space</kbd> or a digit adds a candidate, <kbd>←</kbd> <kbd>→</kbd> move, <kbd>↑</kbd> <kbd>↓</kbd> turn the page, <kbd>Esc</kbd> clears.
strokes.rule: A code is the first four strokes and the last one. A character of fewer strokes spells them all.
strokes.key.s: vertical, vertical with hook, and the curved strokes and hooks like the left of 犭 (竖、竖钩、弯笔、弯钩)
strokes.key.z: every other turning stroke, with vertical-rise and curved-rise (折、竖提、弯提)
strokes.key.b: typed after a radical's strokes, so a radical stands apart from the character it resembles (部)
strokes.note: Jurchen has no agreed stroke order. The table's authors say its codes may not match how you would write a character, so try another order when one fails.
reading.intro: The readings of Jin Qizong's Nüzhenwen Cidian (1984), recorded by Unicode for 806 characters. Type phonetic letters or plain ones: e for ə, s or sh for ʃ, j or zh for dʒ, c or ch for tʃ, h for x and ç.
reading.label: Reading
draw.intro: Draw the character. After each stroke the closest glyphs appear.
draw.note: This compares where your ink lies with one printed face. It has not been measured against real handwriting, so a brush form or a different stroke shape can miss. If you can count strokes, the Strokes page is surer.
draw.failed: The glyphs could not be loaded.
draw.empty: Draw a stroke to see candidates.
draw.keys: Arrow keys move, <kbd>Enter</kbd> adds, <kbd>Esc</kbd> clears the pad.

about.lead: Where each record on this site comes from, and what is still missing.
about.unicodeTitle: Characters, radicals, strokes, readings and numbers
about.unicode: JurchenSources.txt of Unicode 18.0 (Unicode Terms of Use) lists 914 characters with their radical, stroke count and source. 806 carry the reading from Jin Qizong 金啓孮, Nüzhenwen Cidian 女真文辞典 (1984), and 30 a numeric value. The other sources it cites are the Berlin copy of the Sino-Jurchen Vocabulary, Jin Guangping and Jin Qizong (1980), and WG2 N5131.
about.table: The Alari Jurchen Rime table by Yehenara Ayasala, Sulfa and Tunggiya Uju, version 2026.05.29, from 朝花·夕拾, retrieved 2026-11-05. It gives 1,502 codes to the characters, radicals and variants. It states no licence. One code had a stray variation selector, which is removed here.
about.font: Alari Xuwasun Jurchen, public beta of 2026-10-12, by Sulfa, Dooran and Raxon7, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. It is the only font found that draws these code points under an open licence. Its makers describe it as a Fangsong restyling of the forms in the encoding proposal, built on Zhuque Fangsong, and say the forms of the surviving texts are still to be studied.
about.variants: The font holds 537 variants beside the base forms. Alari reaches them with variation selectors VS1 to VS5, numbered from the proposal's order, and with the style sets ss01 to ss05. Unicode 18 registers neither, so a text with these sequences needs this font to show them.
about.encodings: Each card lists the codes the character had before Unicode 18, linked through WG2 N5207 and WG2 N5261R: the X-references of China's proposals, the Private Use code points of the Zhonghua Ziku font, and those of Andrew West's BabelStone scan fonts. The tables and how each link was made are in data/encodings/.
about.convert: The Convert page and src/convert.js read the tables above. Codes with no link, and any code two characters share, stay as they are and are listed.
about.missing: Meanings: only the numerals have one, as Unicode's numeric values. No open table ties glosses to these code points, so none are shown and meanings cannot be searched. Attested lines: no open transcription of the inscriptions or the Sino-Jurchen Vocabulary at these code points was found.
about.howStrokes: The typed letters narrow the codes from the start of the code. The exact code comes first, then the shortest. A code often names several characters, so the candidates are numbered and paged.
about.howReading: Readings and queries are folded to plain letters before they are compared, and a reading that matches as written counts as exact. Exact matches come first, then those that begin with the query, then those that contain it.
about.howDraw: A drawing and each glyph are fitted to a 32×32 square and compared by how far their lines lie apart and how they run. The glyphs are the pen lines of the one face here.
about.howRadicals: Each character sits under the radical Unicode gives it. Numbers follow Unicode's radical order, and stroke counts are Unicode's totals for the character.
about.markText: U+18E01, read tumən in Jin Qizong's dictionary, with the numeric value 10,000 in Unicode.
about.kept: Your text, recent picks, theme and language stay in this browser's storage. The site records nothing and has no analytics.
about.footer: The code of this site is MIT-licensed. The sources above keep their own terms.

card.origin.jin-identical: Written as Chinese {char} in Jin inscriptions. The Ming vocabulary adds a stroke or dot.
card.origin.imitates: Clearly imitates the regular script of Chinese {char}.
card.origin.khitan: Set beside the Khitan large script character for {char}. Study of this link is still at an early stage.
card.origin.chinese-meaning: Altered from Chinese {char}, keeping its meaning.
card.origin.chinese-sound: Altered from Chinese {char}, keeping its sound and not its meaning.
card.origin.numeral: Thought, like all Jurchen numerals, to be a modified Chinese character (Kiyose). West finds some based on the Chinese number, and none plainly from Khitan.
card.origin.none: No source open to this site says where this character comes from.
